parole.significato: forms diminutives of nouns and adjectives; -ette; -let; -et
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian -etto, from Late Latin -ittus. Doublet of -ito, -ete, and -eta.

parole.significato: a clergyman from Italy or France, or that has resided there.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian abate. Doublet of abad.

parole.significato: aria (a musical piece written typically for a solo voice with orchestral accompaniment in an opera or cantata)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian aria.
Borrowed from Italian artigiano.
Borrowed from Italian balcone, ultimately of Germanic origin.
Borrowed from Italian bacchetta.
Borrowed from Italian becco, from Latin beccus (“beak”) because of a medieval gown worn that covered the face like a beak.
Borrowed from Italian bisogno, from Vulgar Latin *bisonium, borrowed from Frankish *bisunnija.

parole.significato: bowl (ball thrown in the game of bowls)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian boccia, from Vulgar Latin *buttia, borrowed from Byzantine Greek βούττια (boúttia, plural of βούττιον (boúttion)), from Ancient Greek βοῦττις (boûttis), possibly borrowed from Pre-Greek.
Borrowed from Italian brillare.
Borrowed from Italian bronzo, from Latin aes Brandusi "bronze of Brindisi", the city in Italy having been famous for the metal.

parole.significato: compass (device used to determine the cardinal directions)
parole.testo: From Italian bùssola (compare French boussole), from Vulgar Latin *buxula, a diminutive form of Late Latin buxis (“box”), from Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís, “boxwood box, box”), from πύξος (púxos, “boxwood”). Apparently influenced by Spanish bruja (“witch”).
Borrowed from Italian busto, from Latin bustum (literally “burned body”).

Borrowed from Italian campione, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin campiō, campiōnem (“champion, fighter”), from Frankish *kampijō (or a Lombardic equivalent) from Proto-Germanic *kampijô, based on Latin campus (“level ground”).
Borrowed from Italian cappello, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus. Doublet of capillo, which was inherited, and of chapeo and chapó, which came via French.

parole.significato: caricature (pictorial representation of someone for comic effect)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian caricatura (“caricature”), from caricare (“carry”), from Late Latin carricāre (“carry”), from Latin carrus (“wagon”), from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Indo-European *kr̥s-o-, from Proto-Indo-European *k̑ers- (“to run”).
Borrowed from Italian carmelita, from Latin carmelītes.
Borrowed from Italian cascata, from cascare (“to fall”), based on Latin cāsus (“fallen”).
Borrowed from Italian catafalco.
Borrowed from Italian ciullo, a now-obsolete shortening of Italian fanciullo, a diminutive based ultimately on Latin īnfāns.
Borrowed from Italian cicerone.
Borrowed from Italian coda, from Latin cauda.
Borrowed from Italian collina, from Late Latin collīna, from the feminine of Latin collīnus, from collis (“hill”) + -ina, from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“top, hill, rock”).
Borrowed from Italian comandare, from Latin commandāre, variant of commendāre. Doublet of encomendar.
From Italian condottiere, from condotta, from Latin conductus.
Borrowed from Italian credenza (possibly through a Catalan intermediate), from Medieval Latin credentia, from Latin credēns. creencia.

parole.significato: cupola, dome (dome-shaped ornamental structure located on top of a larger roof or dome)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian cupola, from Late Latin cupula (“small cask, burying vault”), diminutive of Latin cūpa (“tub, cask”).
Borrowed from Italian disegnare, from Latin designāre. Doublet of designar.
Borrowed from Italian, from divertire (“to amuse, to entertain”), from Latin dīvertere. Cognate to Spanish divertimiento.
Borrowed from Italian despota, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “master, absolute ruler”).

From Northern Italian salada, salata (compare insalata), from Vulgar Latin *salāta, from *salāre, from Latin saliō, from sal (“salt”). Cognates include Italian insalata, Portuguese salada, and French salade.
Borrowed from Italian scarola, scariola, from Late Latin ēscāriola.

Borrowed from Italian scoglio, from Vulgar Latin *scoculum (possibly through a Gallo-Italic intermediate), from Latin scopulus, from Ancient Greek σκόπελος (skópelos, “lookout place: hence peak, headland, promontory”). Compare Catalan escull.
Borrowed from Italian stroppiare, from Latin turpis whence (English turpitude).
Borrowed from Italian faccia (“face”).
Borrowed from Italian forte. Doublet of fuerte.
Borrowed from Italian fracasso, from fracassare, from Latin īnfra- + Vulgar Latin *cassāre, from Latin cassus.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Gaeta
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian gaetano, from Latin Caiētānus. Equivalent to Gaeta + -ano.
Borrowed from Italian gamba, from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin gamba, camba (“leg”), from Ancient Greek καμπή (kampḗ, “bending”).
Borrowed from Italian gavetta, from Latin găbata.
Borrowed from Italian grosso.
Borrowed from Italian gruppo, from Vulgar Latin *cruppus. Compare Renaissance Latin grupus.
Borrowed from Italian influenza, from Latin īnfluentia. Doublet of influencia.
Borrowed from Italian lavorare. Doublet of labrar and laborar.
Borrowed from Italian lasagna.

Borrowed from Italian lava, from Neapolitan and Sicilian lava (“lava; downpour overflowing the streets”), likely from Latin lābēs (“a fall; a collapse; subsidence”), from lābī (“to fall; to slip”); compare lābīna (“landslide”).
Borrowed from Italian letame, from Latin laetāmen (“dung, manure”) < laetus (“happy, rich, also later fertile”).
Borrowed from Italian lira, from Latin libra. Doublet of libra.
Borrowed from Italian maneggiare. Displaced the older Spanish manear, itself of the same origin (Vulgar Latin *manizāre). Compare English manage.

Borrowed from Italian medaglia (originally "half a denarius"), from Early Medieval Latin medālia, ultimately from Latin medius. Doublet of meaja, the native Spanish counterpart. Related to English medal, ultimately from the same Italian source.
Borrowed from Italian mercato. Doublet of mercado.
Directly from Italian minestrone, from minestra (“soup”, ultimately from Latin ministrō) + -one (augmentative suffix).
From Italian miniare, from Latin miniāre, from minium.

parole.significato: model (a successful example to be copied)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian modello.
Borrowed from Italian mofeta (“pestilential exhalation”) and moffetta (“skunk”), from Latin mephitis (“sulphurous exhalation”), from which English mephitic descended.

Borrowed from Italian mosaico, from Medieval Latin musaicum, from Late Latin musivum (opus), from Latin museum, musaeum, probably from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses, (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).
Borrowed from Italian mostaccio.
Unadapted borrowing from Italian mozzarella.

parole.significato: large wall built to protect cities or territories
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian muraglia, from Late Latin muralia, from Latin muralis.
Borrowed from Italian nonna.
Borrowed from Italian novella (“tale”).
Borrowed from Italian ostro. Doublet of austro.
Unadapted borrowing from Italian palazzo, from Latin palātium (“palace, large residence”), from Palātium (“Palatine”), one of the seven hills of Rome. Doublet of palacio and pazo.

parole.significato: of, from or relating to the city of Palermo, Sicily, Italy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian palermitano, from Latin Panormitānus, from Panormus + -itānus.
Borrowed from Italian panatella, diminutive of panata, a derivation of Latin pānis (“bread”).
Borrowed from Italian parlare.
Borrowed from Italian parola, from Latin parabola.

Borrowed from Italian pagliaccio, from Latin palea (“chaff”), whence British English paillasse (“bed made of straw”) and general English pallet (“bed made of straw or hay used in medieval times”). Compare Portuguese palhaço.

parole.significato: overalls, dungarees (loose fitting pair of pants with supporting cross-straps and a panel of material in the chest)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian petto (“chest, breast”), from Latin pectus (whence also Spanish pecho).
Borrowed from Italian piccione, from Latin pīpiōnem. Compare English pigeon.
Pseudo-Italianism, constructed from Italian pippione (“squab, young pigeon”) and -olo (diminutive), the former from Latin pīpiōnem (“squab, young pigeon”), ultimately onomatopoeic.
Borrowed from Italian pecora (“sheep”), from Latin pecora, neuter plural of pecus (“cattle”).
Borrowed from Italian pergola.
Borrowed from Italian regge (“church doors”), from Late Latin (porta) rēgia (literally “kingly door”).
Borrowed from Italian ramolaccio, from Latin armoracia, from Gaulish *are more (“about/around the sea”). Compare German Meerrettich.
Borrowed from Italian ritratto.
Borrowed from Italian salciccia, variant of salsiccia, derived from Latin salsus (“salty”).
Borrowed from Italian selvatico, from Latin silvāticus. Doublet of salvaje. More at selva.
Borrowed from Italian serenata, from the adjective sereno (“clear, calm”), from Latin serēnus (“calm”).
Borrowed from Italian soffitto, from Vulgar Latin *suffīctus, perfect passive participle of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten or fix onto”); compare Classical suffīxus.
Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superanus, from Latin super. Doublet of soberano.
Probably borrowed from Italian tagliare, from Late Latin taliāre. Doublet of tajar, which was inherited from Latin. Compare English tally.
Borrowed from Italian terremoto or Latin terraemōtus.
Borrowed from Italian torso, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”). Doublet of tirso and possibly trozo.
Borrowed from Italian traffico (“traffic”), from Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcāre (“to rub across”). Doublet of tráfico, a borrowing.

parole.significato: trio, threesome (a group of three, especially for performance art)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian trio.
From Italian tombolo (“pillow”), from Latin tumulus (“mound”), from tumeō (“to swell”).
Borrowed from Italian valigia, from Late Latin valisia.
Unadapted borrowing from Italian vendetta (“revenge”), from Latin vindicta. Doublet of vindicta, borrowed from Latin.
Borrowed from Italian vespa. Doublet of avispa.

parole.significato: virtuoso (exhibiting the ability of a virtuoso)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian virtuoso, from Latin virtuōsus (“virtuous”).
Borrowed from Italian vulcano from Latin Vulcanus (“Vulcan”), from Etruscan [script needed] (Velchans).
Borrowed from Italian opera, from Latin opera (“work, labor”). Doublet of obra and huebra.
